records.answer: ARIA 0.1 exercises a method for evaluating AI applications through scenarios, human interaction and structured assessment. Its report makes the evaluation process inspectable. It is not an operating authorization, a general safety certificate or evidence of sustained mission benefit.
records.scope: The existing, bounded NIST ARIA 0.1 evaluation pilot. The wider ARIA program, future iterations, seven submitted applications and participating organizations are not additional project identities here.
records.stage: Multi-level evaluation pilot; continuous system assurance and operating outcomes remain unadmitted

The report does not admit a named deployment's authorization, incident response, corrective action or comparable mission outcomes. This review is AI author self-review, not an independent assessment of the evaluated applications.
records.counting_note: This is the same single eligible ARIA 0.1 pilot. Applications, scenarios, organizations and testing sessions are not counted as additional projects.

timeline.event: The pilot report dates the ARIA program launch to May 2024; no exact launch day is supplied in the inspected passage.

NIST's publication page dates release of the pilot report to November 13, 2025.

sections.heading: The pilot is the unit of account
sections.text: NIST's publication record identifies five submitting organizations and seven AI applications. It describes three scenarios: TV Spoilers, Meal Planner and Pathfinder. These provide bounded evaluation settings, not a census of operational AI. The portfolio therefore counts the identified pilot once. Neither the number of applications nor the number of scenarios is a measure of deployed systems or public benefit.

sections.heading: Three testing levels answer different questions
sections.text: The program pairs model testing, red teaming and field testing to examine technical and contextual behaviour. Its stated aim is to produce methods and metrics that inform decisions. Our interpretation is that an evaluator should preserve the testing mode with each finding: behaviour under adversarial prompting and behaviour during a user's task are not interchangeable evidence. A program intention is not a completed assurance decision.

sections.heading: Trace the result back to the observation
sections.text: The report connects testing dialogues and questionnaires to assessment and then the Contextual Robustness Index, or CoRIx. The pilot focuses on validity: whether output meets intended-use requirements. Higher reported scores indicate less validity, not a better grade. This makes score direction and the measured construct essential context. We do not turn the instrument into a single general-safety ranking.

sections.heading: Keep coverage limits beside the method
sections.text: The report describes 508 testing sessions and English-language scenarios. Not every application was tested at all three levels; most were submitted for one scenario, and the reported results use a subset. Those limits prevent treating the sessions as a balanced comparison of all applications. Generalising to another language, task or deployment would require evidence beyond this pilot.

sections.heading: A schedule is not a results publication
sections.text: The program homepage still shows a timetable from December 2024 testing through a summer 2025 summary. That schedule is retained as schedule context; the separate publication record dates this report to November 13, 2025. Inspection on November 22, 2026 does not make the report new or verify every scheduled event. Future program plans are not outcomes already achieved.

sections.heading: The missing bridge to operating assurance
sections.text: For a deployed system, our next evidence requirement is an exact application version, use context and owner authorization tied to monitoring, incidents and corrective actions. A meaningful outcome comparison also needs a defined population, baseline and observation period. These are editorial admission criteria, not additional findings from the pilot. The pilot's method can inform that work without substituting for independent review or the owner's operating decision.

next_artifacts: A named system/version evaluation and owner authorization with an explicit use context.
Linked monitoring, incident and corrective-action records rather than a one-off score.
A stable outcome definition, baseline, population and period before comparing mission benefits.

sections.heading: Power and stored energy answer different questions

records.answer: ARIA 0.1 exercises a method for evaluating AI applications through scenarios, human interaction and structured assessment. Its report makes the evaluation process inspectable. It is not an operating authorization, a general safety certificate or evidence of sustained mission benefit.
records.scope: The existing, bounded NIST ARIA 0.1 evaluation pilot. The wider ARIA program, future iterations, seven submitted applications and participating organizations are not additional project identities here.
records.stage: Multi-level evaluation pilot; continuous system assurance and operating outcomes remain unadmitted
records.decision_boundary: The established Phase 61 evaluation-before-continuous-assurance stage is retained. The report does not admit a named deployment's authorization, incident response, corrective action or comparable mission outcomes. This review is AI author self-review, not an independent assessment of the evaluated applications.
records.counting_note: This is the same single eligible ARIA 0.1 pilot. Applications, scenarios, organizations and testing sessions are not counted as additional projects.

timeline.event: The pilot report dates the ARIA program launch to May 2024; no exact launch day is supplied in the inspected passage.

sections.heading: The pilot is the unit of account
sections.text: NIST's publication record identifies five submitting organizations and seven AI applications. It describes three scenarios: TV Spoilers, Meal Planner and Pathfinder. These provide bounded evaluation settings, not a census of operational AI. The portfolio therefore counts the identified pilot once. Neither the number of applications nor the number of scenarios is a measure of deployed systems or public benefit.

sections.heading: Three testing levels answer different questions
sections.text: The program pairs model testing, red teaming and field testing to examine technical and contextual behaviour. Its stated aim is to produce methods and metrics that inform decisions. Our interpretation is that an evaluator should preserve the testing mode with each finding: behaviour under adversarial prompting and behaviour during a user's task are not interchangeable evidence. A program intention is not a completed assurance decision.

sections.heading: Trace the result back to the observation
sections.text: The report connects testing dialogues and questionnaires to assessment and then the Contextual Robustness Index, or CoRIx. The pilot focuses on validity: whether output meets intended-use requirements. Higher reported scores indicate less validity, not a better grade. This makes score direction and the measured construct essential context. We do not turn the instrument into a single general-safety ranking.

sections.heading: Keep coverage limits beside the method
sections.text: The report describes 508 testing sessions and English-language scenarios. Not every application was tested at all three levels; most were submitted for one scenario, and the reported results use a subset. Those limits prevent treating the sessions as a balanced comparison of all applications. Generalising to another language, task or deployment would require evidence beyond this pilot.

sections.heading: A schedule is not a results publication
sections.text: The program homepage still shows a timetable from December 2024 testing through a summer 2025 summary. That schedule is retained as schedule context; the separate publication record dates this report to November 13, 2025. Inspection on November 22, 2026 does not make the report new or verify every scheduled event. Future program plans are not outcomes already achieved.

sections.heading: The missing bridge to operating assurance
sections.text: For a deployed system, our next evidence requirement is an exact application version, use context and owner authorization tied to monitoring, incidents and corrective actions. A meaningful outcome comparison also needs a defined population, baseline and observation period. These are editorial admission criteria, not additional findings from the pilot. The pilot's method can inform that work without substituting for independent review or the owner's operating decision.

next_artifacts: A named system/version evaluation and owner authorization with an explicit use context.
Linked monitoring, incident and corrective-action records rather than a one-off score.

sections.heading: A shared site does not have one operating status
sections.text: Vistra's report for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 says the 300 MW and 100 MW batteries will not return to service. It separately describes a potential restart of the 350 MW facility as still under evaluation. These are the operator's component-specific statements, not a declaration that the whole site has restarted. The gas plant and the separate Elkhorn battery cannot supply an operating result for this storage account.

sections.heading: Who is responsible for the cleanup
sections.text: EPA's response page describes Vistra as performing and paying for battery removal under federal oversight. EPA's remit includes removal within the fence and preparation for transport; state and local authorities retain outside-the-fence responsibilities and other on-site matters. The July 17, 2025 agreement therefore establishes a removal obligation and oversight relationship. It is not evidence that all batteries have been removed, that every historical audit item is closed or that the facility is accepted for operation.

sections.heading: The September fire was not a restarted battery service
sections.text: EPA records the September 18 fire in the already damaged Moss Landing 300 building. Its later explanation says the building had no active storage operations and its batteries were not connected to the grid; remaining modules could nevertheless retain charge. EPA describes the exact cause of this September incident as unknown. The incident shows why stopping dispatch and removing a residual fire hazard are different tasks, without establishing a general failure rate for battery storage.

sections.heading: Final phase does not mean finished
sections.text: EPA's September 8 announcement describes demolition and treatment of previously inaccessible material and projects removal and demolition completion in mid-2027. That is a forecast. Vistra's November 12 update says removal of the final intact batteries has begun, with damaged material and debris to follow. These statements concern different work packages and dates. Neither should be compressed into a completed-cleanup claim or used to award an operating-recovery stage.

sections.heading: Monitoring and laboratory samples need separate interpretation

records.title: Manatee storage: capacity, monthly operation and a changing battery fleet
records.answer: Manatee is an existing, owner-reported in-service battery, not just an announced capacity project. Its 409 MW power rating and 900 MWh energy rating describe different capabilities. The retained monthly record provides operating evidence, while interval availability, measured customer savings and the original retirement proposal remain separate questions.
records.scope: One Florida Power & Light battery facility at Parrish, Manatee County, Florida. The adjacent solar facility, older thermal units, other FPL batteries and the Florida utility-storage system are related but distinct objects. The EIA plant label used in the earlier monthly acquisition does not turn every resource at the site into this battery.
records.stage: Owner-reported in service; retained monthly evidence; interval availability remains unresolved

timeline.event: FPL announced that construction had begun and described anticipated storage, savings and retirement benefits. These were prospective claims at that date.
FPL announced commissioning and described the battery as newly operational, with 409 MW of power and 900 MWh of stored energy.
The 2026–2035 site plan was submitted to the Florida Public Service Commission. Its battery-storage narrative retains Manatee's end-2021 in-service history; the plan is not a new commissioning event.
The inspected EIA release index dates publication of August 2026 monthly data here. This is a dataset-release date, not an additional Manatee operating observation in this account.
FPL announced commissioning of the separate Lansing Smith battery and called it the company's largest by energy capacity. The announcement changes fleet context, not Manatee's identity or rating.

sections.heading: Power and stored energy answer different questions
sections.text: FPL describes Manatee as a 409 MW / 900 MWh battery at Parrish, charged from the nearby Manatee Solar Energy Center. MW measures rated power; MWh measures stored energy. Dividing the two published ratings gives about 2.20 hours at rated power as nameplate arithmetic, not a measured discharge test or an availability guarantee. The owner's household-equivalent illustration depends on assumed household demand and should not be treated as the number of customers continuously served. The solar plant and battery have different functions even when their location and charging relationship are shared.

sections.heading: Commissioning does not settle the retirement account
sections.text: The January 2021 construction announcement linked the battery and other modernization work to anticipated retirement of older gas units, fuel savings and emissions reductions. FPL's December announcement then established an owner-reported commissioning milestone. It did not establish all the forecast benefits. The April 2026 plan's note on Manatee Units 1 and 2 describes them as winter-peaking units staffed and operated for extreme winter demand. That later qualification matters: the earlier retirement proposal is not proof that both units were permanently retired. No measured avoided-emissions or customer-savings total is derived here.

sections.heading: Read fleet plans with their reporting dates
sections.text: The April 2026 plan describes 991 MW of large-scale installed battery storage across FPL's system, including Manatee and other facilities. That is a fleet snapshot in a planning document, not Manatee's available power or a statewide outcome. Later installations can change the fleet total without changing this facility's identity. The plan's future additions are forecasts; they must not be counted as already operating assets or used as a denominator for Manatee's performance.

sections.heading: Monthly data are evidence, but not an availability series
sections.text: The earlier monthly acquisition is retained below with its actual July review date. It should not be erased by describing all operating evidence as missing. EIA's current release index covers monthly and annual plant-level statistics and, on this inspection, lists August 2026 data released on October 23. The ZIP workbook was not newly extracted in this review, so this account does not add June–August observations or certify revisions to the earlier months. Charging energy, gross output and reported net generation are different fields; their names and reporting periods must be preserved before comparing values.

sections.heading: A larger energy store is not a larger power rating
sections.text: On November 9, 2026, FPL described the separate Lansing Smith facility as 400 MW and 1,600 MWh, with up to four hours of supply. Its claim to be FPL's largest battery by stored-energy capacity is compatible with Manatee's higher 409 MW power rating and lower 900 MWh energy rating. Comparing MWh with MW would produce a false ranking. The new announcement neither expands Manatee nor establishes a global league table. Historical superlatives remain attached to their date and metric, and Lansing Smith is context only in this account.

sections.heading: The next evidence must measure the service being claimed
sections.text: A current rating and monthly totals do not answer whether the battery was available during particular peak intervals, how often it was constrained, or how benefits were allocated to customers. The next useful review should join the exact battery identity to dated interval dispatch and outage or availability records, with a declared denominator and revision policy. It should keep a missing interval separate from a documented zero. Any savings or emissions claim needs a stated comparison case rather than conversion of a construction forecast into a measured result. These are editorial evidence requirements, not a finding that those records do not exist.

retained_evidence.statement: The retained July 25 acquisition identified the energy-storage worksheet's Manatee Solar Energy Center row, plant 60014, and recorded monthly charging energy, gross generation and reported net generation for January–May 2026. Those are earlier saved findings, not a new workbook inspection or a new governed operating-series admission.

sections.heading: Commissioning and capacity have their own dates
sections.text: The August 2020 announcement's headline describes a 250 MW project, while its body reports 230 MW operating and targets the remaining capacity for month-end. The repeated portfolio tables describe the same asset, not two batteries. Power in MW also cannot supply an energy rating or storage duration without a compatible MWh figure.

sections.heading: Partial return is not full restoration
sections.text: The final November 2025 resolution describes Gateway as partly back online while the fire-affected building remained offline. Newer capacity was supplying resource-adequacy obligations associated with the unavailable portion. That is meaningful operating context and must not be erased by calling the entire facility continuously offline. It is nevertheless a historical account, not a current full-capacity availability series.

sections.heading: Cleanup obligations and completed cleanup differ
sections.text: EPA's announcement assigns cleanup costs and work to Gateway, including monitoring during battery handling, safe removal and disposal, and work plans and reporting. The response profile identifies the same San Diego site but does not supply a new publication date. A cleanup order establishes responsibilities, not their completion. The administrative-record detail page returned headings without document rows in this review; that retrieval limit cannot establish that closeout records do not exist. Final cleanup acceptance and a final incident finding remain separate artifacts.

sections.heading: Audit findings and the owner response have different authority
sections.text: The June 2025 CPUC audit produced sixteen findings; its letter followed in August. In its response, Gateway claimed fourteen closed and two remaining, with an introductory end-October target. The detailed response instead gives Finding 1 a December 31, 2025 target and Finding 7 an October 24 target. Preserve that discrepancy rather than silently harmonizing the dates. These are operator claims and plans, not independent regulator acceptance or current closure status. The catalog's June 2026 Gateway Generating Station listing concerns a different facility.

sections.heading: The amended contract sets future obligations
sections.text: Resolution E-5428 approved the amended Gateway contract. It sets expected initial delivery for June 1, 2027 and a deadline of August 1, 2027. Neither date is an observed restart or completed delivery. A contract obligation, facility nameplate rating and the capacity actually available during an interval must retain separate meanings; approval of one does not measure the others.

sections.heading: What would resolve the remaining operating question
sections.text: A useful next account needs a final incident disposition, accepted corrective-action and cleanup records, and the exact restored configuration tied to dated service evidence. An operating series should identify its contracted-capacity denominator, reporting intervals, outages and revisions. A missing interval is not a documented zero; partial operation is not full restoration. These are editorial admission requirements, not a claim that agencies or the operator have published nothing further. The earlier saved evidence boundary remains visible below.

records.scope: One U.S. Air Force F-15EX aircraft production program. Individual aircraft and contract lots are events within this existing identity, not additional projects. This account concerns public acquisition and delivery evidence, not operational employment or a fleet-readiness assessment.
records.stage: Dated production and delivery account; no governed monthly acceptance series admitted

timeline.event: The Air Force's later account places the start of a production-line interruption here, ending November 17; it does not say all delivery activity stopped.
The Air Force account reports delivery of EX14.
The same account reports EX15 delivery and describes EX16 as following less than three weeks later.
The receiving wing's later description dates EX16's arrival to this day. Its relation to the earlier delivery interval remains unreconciled.
The Air Force dates its Lot 7 award announcement for 22 aircraft to this day; DVIDS posted the account September 30.

sections.heading: A larger order is not a delivery count
sections.text: The Air Force's September 29, 2026 announcement reports a Lot 7 contract for 22 aircraft. Boeing's same-day account states that Lots 1–7 now cover 120 aircraft under contract and gives the new award's value as $2.38 billion. These are acquisition quantities and a supplier-reported contract value, not a count of aircraft formally accepted that month. The award supports future production; it does not establish when every contracted aircraft will be received.

sections.heading: Follow the separate institutional decisions
sections.text: The Air Force announcement describes negotiation among its program, contracting, pricing, engineering, financial and logistics teams and Boeing. It says the agreement retained 22 aircraft within available funding while accounting for the 2025 disruption and inflation. That is the acquisition office's account of the award, not an independent cost audit. The earlier recovery story names the program office, manufacturer and Defense Contract Management Agency. Their involvement does not make every event in a news release a formally documented acceptance.

sections.heading: Keep the interruption and arrival accounts together
sections.text: The December 2025 Air Force story describes a production interruption from August 4 through November 17 while also reporting deliveries inside that interval. Its relative timing for EX16 does not align with the receiving wing's December 11 arrival if both describe the same milestone after EX15's November 16 delivery. That comparison is an editorial inference, not an issuer correction. The wing page is dated February 17, 2026; its description concerns the earlier arrival. No video was viewed or transcribed.

sections.heading: A target rate still needs repeated observations
sections.text: Boeing's September 2026 account identifies EX22 as its first Lot 3 delivery and says it is working toward production of two aircraft per month. A delivery announcement and a target rate are different evidence. The aircraft identifier is not a cumulative accepted-aircraft count, and the contract total is not the numerator for a monthly rate. The selected sources do not provide all formal-acceptance events, including months with none. They therefore cannot establish whether the target was consistently achieved.

sections.heading: What changed since the earlier reading

records.title: GSA post-quantum acquisition: buying a transition is not completing one
records.answer: GSA provides acquisition guidance and is developing identity-testing capability. These are enabling steps, not a named agency's completed migration. This account follows the handoff from requirements and purchasing to the system-specific evidence needed for acceptance and retirement.
records.scope: The existing GSA procurement-guidance account, with related federal identity and physical-access context. It is not an umbrella migration project and does not count individual agencies, products or working-group participants as deployments.
records.stage: Procurement and testing context; named migration and operating acceptance remain unadmitted
records.decision_boundary: The existing Phase 61 procurement-before-migration stage is retained. No named order, system cutover, operational acceptance or vulnerable-system retirement is admitted by this bounded review. This does not establish that such artifacts do not exist.
records.counting_note: This retained guidance/context account contributes zero eligible projects. A deeper reading does not turn it into an implementation or add an identity.

timeline.event: Version 1 of the buyer guide is dated June 2025. The document does not supply an exact publication day.
GSA's later August 24 account reports the first FICAM interagency working-group meeting, with 40 participants from 17 agencies; attendance is not a migration count.
GSA publishes its account of FICAM modernization and the PACS lab's developing quantum-resistant testing capability.
The acquisition web page displays this last-updated date. It is a page-maintenance date, not a system acceptance milestone.

sections.heading: Start with a system boundary, not a shopping list
sections.text: The June 2025 guide is written for agency acquisition and technology teams. Its sequence connects inventory, assessment, planning, implementation and maintenance. For this account, the useful next question is which named system is changing, who owns it and what evidence will show the change worked. A purchase without that boundary cannot establish which vulnerable dependencies were actually removed.

sections.heading: Separate the purchaser from the acquisition enabler
sections.text: GSA's current acquisition page assigns inventory and migration planning to agencies. It describes GSA's role in requirements, contract vehicles, vendor visibility and cloud-service posture, including MAS, GWACs and EIS. This division matters: an available purchasing channel does not identify an agency order or prove that a purchased component has been integrated successfully. The page is institutional context, not an order register.

sections.heading: Identity testing is a different object from deployment
sections.text: The August 24 account says GSA is updating FICAM and expanding the PACS lab's capacity to evaluate quantum-resistant building-access solutions. It describes incorporation of algorithms into testing as beginning. The reported August 12 working-group meeting shows coordination, not migrated credentials or buildings. This account does not infer that an updated test, an approved product, an installed system and an accepted operating service are equivalent.

sections.heading: Plan for the transition after the contract
sections.text: The buyer guide discusses testing, system interdependencies, hybrid approaches and continuing maintenance. Its emphasis on crypto-agility recognises that migration is not simply a one-time equipment swap. Our editorial implication is to retain each system's test configuration, compatibility exceptions and rollback conditions alongside its acquisition record. Those are proposed evidence requirements here, not claims that GSA has published a completed agency test package.

sections.heading: Read dates according to what happened
sections.text: The guide's June 2025 version date, the working group's reported August 12 meeting, the August 24 blog and the acquisition page's September 22 update describe different objects. November 22 is our inspection date. None should be substituted for a contract award, cutover or acceptance date. Existing policy-source history remains intact; this review does not reissue deadlines or certify agency compliance.

sections.heading: What would justify a new implementation account
sections.text: An agency-specific account should link its system inventory and procurement to an identified product configuration, interoperability tests, a controlled cutover and an owner acceptance decision. Remaining vulnerable services and retirement evidence must be visible, with exceptions rather than an implied universal success. These are editorial admission requirements. Until that chain is supported, the guide remains valuable context and contributes zero projects to the portfolio target.

next_artifacts: A named agency/system inventory and procurement artifact with an exact scope and accountable owner.
System-specific test, cutover and acceptance records, including exceptions and rollback conditions.
Evidence identifying which vulnerable systems or cryptographic uses were retired and which remain.

records.title: NIST ARIA 0.1: what the evaluation pilot measures, and what it does not
records.answer: ARIA 0.1 exercises a method for evaluating AI applications through scenarios, human interaction and structured assessment. Its report makes the evaluation process inspectable. It is not an operating authorization, a general safety certificate or evidence of sustained mission benefit.
records.scope: The existing, bounded NIST ARIA 0.1 evaluation pilot. The wider ARIA program, future iterations, seven submitted applications and participating organizations are not additional project identities here.
records.stage: Multi-level evaluation pilot; continuous system assurance and operating outcomes remain unadmitted
records.decision_boundary: The established Phase 61 evaluation-before-continuous-assurance stage is retained. The report does not admit a named deployment's authorization, incident response, corrective action or comparable mission outcomes. This review is AI author self-review, not an independent assessment of the evaluated applications.
records.counting_note: This is the same single eligible ARIA 0.1 pilot. Applications, scenarios, organizations and testing sessions are not counted as additional projects.

timeline.event: The pilot report dates the ARIA program launch to May 2024; no exact launch day is supplied in the inspected passage.
The report's publication-history page records NIST Editorial Review Board approval on this day; that is publication review, not system operating authorization.
NIST's publication page dates release of the pilot report to November 13, 2025.

sections.heading: The pilot is the unit of account
sections.text: NIST's publication record identifies five submitting organizations and seven AI applications. It describes three scenarios: TV Spoilers, Meal Planner and Pathfinder. These provide bounded evaluation settings, not a census of operational AI. The portfolio therefore counts the identified pilot once. Neither the number of applications nor the number of scenarios is a measure of deployed systems or public benefit.

sections.heading: Three testing levels answer different questions
sections.text: The program pairs model testing, red teaming and field testing to examine technical and contextual behaviour. Its stated aim is to produce methods and metrics that inform decisions. Our interpretation is that an evaluator should preserve the testing mode with each finding: behaviour under adversarial prompting and behaviour during a user's task are not interchangeable evidence. A program intention is not a completed assurance decision.

sections.heading: Trace the result back to the observation
sections.text: The report connects testing dialogues and questionnaires to assessment and then the Contextual Robustness Index, or CoRIx. The pilot focuses on validity: whether output meets intended-use requirements. Higher reported scores indicate less validity, not a better grade. This makes score direction and the measured construct essential context. We do not turn the instrument into a single general-safety ranking.

sections.heading: Keep coverage limits beside the method
sections.text: The report describes 508 testing sessions and English-language scenarios. Not every application was tested at all three levels; most were submitted for one scenario, and the reported results use a subset. Those limits prevent treating the sessions as a balanced comparison of all applications. Generalising to another language, task or deployment would require evidence beyond this pilot.

sections.heading: A schedule is not a results publication
sections.text: The program homepage still shows a timetable from December 2024 testing through a summer 2025 summary. That schedule is retained as schedule context; the separate publication record dates this report to November 13, 2025. Inspection on November 22, 2026 does not make the report new or verify every scheduled event. Future program plans are not outcomes already achieved.

sections.heading: The missing bridge to operating assurance
sections.text: For a deployed system, our next evidence requirement is an exact application version, use context and owner authorization tied to monitoring, incidents and corrective actions. A meaningful outcome comparison also needs a defined population, baseline and observation period. These are editorial admission criteria, not additional findings from the pilot. The pilot's method can inform that work without substituting for independent review or the owner's operating decision.

next_artifacts: A named system/version evaluation and owner authorization with an explicit use context.
Linked monitoring, incident and corrective-action records rather than a one-off score.
A stable outcome definition, baseline, population and period before comparing mission benefits.

records.title: Moss Landing: battery removal, another fire and separate restart decisions
records.answer: Battery removal at Vistra's Moss Landing site remains distinct from restored storage service. The September 2026 fire involved batteries left in the damaged 300 MW building, not a restarted grid-connected system. Vistra's latest quarterly account keeps the 300 MW and 100 MW facilities in closure and leaves a potential 350 MW restart uncertain.
records.scope: One existing Vistra Moss Landing storage-facility account, distinguishing its 300 MW, 100 MW and 350 MW components. The separate Elkhorn asset, the gas plant and California's wider battery system are outside this project count. Cleanup events do not create new projects.
records.stage: Dated cleanup and issuer-reported closure/restart account; no accepted operating recovery or governed conversion stage added
records.decision_boundary: The original Tier B casebook has no governed Phase 61–64 conversion file. This dated narrative does not create one, close the earlier CPUC audit items, admit a performance series or establish a public-health outcome. EPA oversight, operator statements and any future regulator acceptance remain separate.
records.counting_note: The same Vistra facility remains one eligible project. Its three battery components, two fires and cleanup phases are not additional project identities; Elkhorn is excluded.

timeline.event: The fire begins in Vistra's Moss Landing 300 battery building, according to EPA's response record.
EPA's document description dates the agreement under which Vistra performs and pays for battery removal under EPA oversight.
EPA announces the final removal phase and describes mid-2027 as a projected completion period, not a completed cleanup.
EPA records another fire in the damaged building and a precautionary shelter-in-place order. It is a separate incident from January 2025.
Vistra signs its report for the quarter ended September 30. This signature date is not the inspection date or an independently verified EDGAR acceptance timestamp.
Vistra reports that removal of the final intact batteries has begun; subsequent removal of damaged materials and debris is still described as future work.

sections.heading: A shared site does not have one operating status
sections.text: Vistra's report for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 says the 300 MW and 100 MW batteries will not return to service. It separately describes a potential restart of the 350 MW facility as still under evaluation. These are the operator's component-specific statements, not a declaration that the whole site has restarted. The gas plant and the separate Elkhorn battery cannot supply an operating result for this storage account.

sections.heading: Who is responsible for the cleanup
sections.text: EPA's response page describes Vistra as performing and paying for battery removal under federal oversight. EPA's remit includes removal within the fence and preparation for transport; state and local authorities retain outside-the-fence responsibilities and other on-site matters. The July 17, 2025 agreement therefore establishes a removal obligation and oversight relationship. It is not evidence that all batteries have been removed, that every historical audit item is closed or that the facility is accepted for operation.

sections.heading: The September fire was not a restarted battery service
sections.text: EPA records the September 18 fire in the already damaged Moss Landing 300 building. Its later explanation says the building had no active storage operations and its batteries were not connected to the grid; remaining modules could nevertheless retain charge. EPA describes the exact cause of this September incident as unknown. The incident shows why stopping dispatch and removing a residual fire hazard are different tasks, without establishing a general failure rate for battery storage.

sections.heading: Final phase does not mean finished
sections.text: EPA's September 8 announcement describes demolition and treatment of previously inaccessible material and projects removal and demolition completion in mid-2027. That is a forecast. Vistra's November 12 update says removal of the final intact batteries has begun, with damaged material and debris to follow. These statements concern different work packages and dates. Neither should be compressed into a completed-cleanup claim or used to award an operating-recovery stage.

sections.heading: Monitoring and laboratory samples need separate interpretation
sections.text: EPA's September-fire FAQ reports perimeter monitoring for particular pollutants and describes additional sampling. Vistra's September 29 update reports nickel slightly above the applicable screening level at one southwest location during the shelter-in-place period, followed by samples without exceedances after the order ended. These are different measures and time windows. The operator's account is attributed, not independently confirmed here: the county page returned HTTP 403. Neither account establishes a site-wide health outcome or an absence of all exposure.

sections.heading: An investigation update is not regulatory acceptance
sections.text: EPA's historical timeline retains a January-entry statement that the cause was being investigated. Vistra's later quarterly filing says its own fire investigation was completed during the third quarter, while still leaving the 350 MW restart uncertain. This does not provide a regulator's causal finding, close the distinct September incident or authorize operation. The next useful records are authority-reviewed findings, documented removal/disposal completion and any component-specific restart acceptance, followed by comparable operating observations.

next_artifacts: Authority-reviewed incident findings and item-specific safety dispositions, with the January 2025 and September 2026 events kept separate.
Battery-removal and disposal completion records that distinguish intact modules, damaged material, debris and any remaining obligations.
A component-specific restart/acceptance decision and comparable subsequent operating evidence before describing restored storage service.

records.title: Manatee storage: capacity, monthly operation and a changing battery fleet
records.answer: Manatee is an existing, owner-reported in-service battery, not just an announced capacity project. Its 409 MW power rating and 900 MWh energy rating describe different capabilities. The retained monthly record provides operating evidence, while interval availability, measured customer savings and the original retirement proposal remain separate questions.
records.scope: One Florida Power & Light battery facility at Parrish, Manatee County, Florida. The adjacent solar facility, older thermal units, other FPL batteries and the Florida utility-storage system are related but distinct objects. The EIA plant label used in the earlier monthly acquisition does not turn every resource at the site into this battery.
records.stage: Owner-reported in service; retained monthly evidence; interval availability remains unresolved

timeline.event: FPL announced that construction had begun and described anticipated storage, savings and retirement benefits. These were prospective claims at that date.
FPL announced commissioning and described the battery as newly operational, with 409 MW of power and 900 MWh of stored energy.
The 2026–2035 site plan was submitted to the Florida Public Service Commission. Its battery-storage narrative retains Manatee's end-2021 in-service history; the plan is not a new commissioning event.
The inspected EIA release index dates publication of August 2026 monthly data here. This is a dataset-release date, not an additional Manatee operating observation in this account.
FPL announced commissioning of the separate Lansing Smith battery and called it the company's largest by energy capacity. The announcement changes fleet context, not Manatee's identity or rating.

sections.heading: Power and stored energy answer different questions
sections.text: FPL describes Manatee as a 409 MW / 900 MWh battery at Parrish, charged from the nearby Manatee Solar Energy Center. MW measures rated power; MWh measures stored energy. Dividing the two published ratings gives about 2.20 hours at rated power as nameplate arithmetic, not a measured discharge test or an availability guarantee. The owner's household-equivalent illustration depends on assumed household demand and should not be treated as the number of customers continuously served. The solar plant and battery have different functions even when their location and charging relationship are shared.

sections.heading: Commissioning does not settle the retirement account
sections.text: The January 2021 construction announcement linked the battery and other modernization work to anticipated retirement of older gas units, fuel savings and emissions reductions. FPL's December announcement then established an owner-reported commissioning milestone. It did not establish all the forecast benefits. The April 2026 plan's note on Manatee Units 1 and 2 describes them as winter-peaking units staffed and operated for extreme winter demand. That later qualification matters: the earlier retirement proposal is not proof that both units were permanently retired. No measured avoided-emissions or customer-savings total is derived here.

sections.heading: Read fleet plans with their reporting dates
sections.text: The April 2026 plan describes 991 MW of large-scale installed battery storage across FPL's system, including Manatee and other facilities. That is a fleet snapshot in a planning document, not Manatee's available power or a statewide outcome. Later installations can change the fleet total without changing this facility's identity. The plan's future additions are forecasts; they must not be counted as already operating assets or used as a denominator for Manatee's performance.

sections.heading: Monthly data are evidence, but not an availability series
sections.text: The earlier monthly acquisition is retained below with its actual July review date. It should not be erased by describing all operating evidence as missing. EIA's current release index covers monthly and annual plant-level statistics and, on this inspection, lists August 2026 data released on October 23. The ZIP workbook was not newly extracted in this review, so this account does not add June–August observations or certify revisions to the earlier months. Charging energy, gross output and reported net generation are different fields; their names and reporting periods must be preserved before comparing values.

sections.heading: A larger energy store is not a larger power rating
sections.text: On November 9, 2026, FPL described the separate Lansing Smith facility as 400 MW and 1,600 MWh, with up to four hours of supply. Its claim to be FPL's largest battery by stored-energy capacity is compatible with Manatee's higher 409 MW power rating and lower 900 MWh energy rating. Comparing MWh with MW would produce a false ranking. The new announcement neither expands Manatee nor establishes a global league table. Historical superlatives remain attached to their date and metric, and Lansing Smith is context only in this account.

sections.heading: The next evidence must measure the service being claimed
sections.text: A current rating and monthly totals do not answer whether the battery was available during particular peak intervals, how often it was constrained, or how benefits were allocated to customers. The next useful review should join the exact battery identity to dated interval dispatch and outage or availability records, with a declared denominator and revision policy. It should keep a missing interval separate from a documented zero. Any savings or emissions claim needs a stated comparison case rather than conversion of a construction forecast into a measured result. These are editorial evidence requirements, not a finding that those records do not exist.

retained_evidence.statement: The retained July 25 acquisition identified the energy-storage worksheet's Manatee Solar Energy Center row, plant 60014, and recorded monthly charging energy, gross generation and reported net generation for January–May 2026. It moved that evidence gap to Partially Closed, while interval dispatch and availability remained unresolved. Those are earlier saved findings, not a new workbook inspection or a new governed operating-series admission.

next_artifacts: The current EIA energy-storage worksheet for the exact plant/battery identity, with a preserved release vintage and an explicit comparison against the retained January–May record.
Named-battery interval dispatch, outage and availability evidence with stable reporting periods, denominators and revision treatment.
Dated unit-disposition and measured cost or emissions evidence before replacing the earlier modernization forecasts with outcome claims.
records.decision_boundary: This Tier B casebook has no governed Phase 61–64 conversion file. The existing July 25 monthly acquisition remains Partially Closed; this account neither downgrades it to no evidence nor upgrades it to interval availability. No new operating series, governed stage, Phase 60 identity or Florida-wide outcome is admitted.
records.counting_note: The same one eligible project is retained. Containers, monthly rows, the neighboring solar plant and the separate Lansing Smith announcement do not add identities to this account.

records.title: Gateway battery storage after the fire
records.answer: Gateway's record includes commissioning, a serious fire, cleanup requirements and a documented partial return to service. Those milestones answer different questions. The unresolved question is full contracted-capacity restoration and its supporting operating record, not whether any operation ever resumed.
records.scope: One battery facility in East Otay Mesa, San Diego County, at 641 Camino De La Fuente. Gateway Generating Station in Antioch is a different facility; neither that plant nor Moss Landing is included in this identity.
records.stage: Partial return documented in 2025; final investigation and full contracted-capacity restoration remain an open evidence question

timeline.event: LS Power reported 230 MW operating and targeted 250 MW by month-end.
The battery fire began; EPA's account records later flare-ups through May 28.
REV's portfolio snapshot lists 250 MW owned net capacity. This is an inventory date, not a restart milestone.
The CPUC field audit began, continuing through June 5.
EPA's news header says July 6; its body dateline says July 7. Both are retained without choosing a substitute date.
The CPUC audit letter identified sixteen findings requiring corrective action.
The CPUC adopted the final contract-amendment resolution.
The resolution's issuance date is separate from adoption and from its historical partial-return account.

sections.heading: Commissioning and capacity have their own dates
sections.text: The August 2020 announcement's headline describes a 250 MW project, while its body reports 230 MW operating and targets the remaining capacity for month-end. REV later lists Gateway at 250 MW owned net capacity in a November 2024 portfolio snapshot. Neither number is a current availability measurement. The repeated portfolio tables describe the same asset, not two batteries. Power in MW also cannot supply an energy rating or storage duration without a compatible MWh figure.

sections.heading: Partial return is not full restoration
sections.text: The final November 2025 resolution describes Gateway as partly back online while the fire-affected building remained offline. Newer capacity was supplying resource-adequacy obligations associated with the unavailable portion. That is meaningful operating context and must not be erased by calling the entire facility continuously offline. It is nevertheless a historical account, not a current full-capacity availability series.

sections.heading: Cleanup obligations and completed cleanup differ
sections.text: EPA's announcement assigns cleanup costs and work to Gateway, including monitoring during battery handling, safe removal and disposal, and work plans and reporting. The response profile identifies the same San Diego site but does not supply a new publication date. A cleanup order establishes responsibilities, not their completion. The administrative-record detail page returned headings without document rows in this review; that retrieval limit cannot establish that closeout records do not exist. Final cleanup acceptance and a final incident finding remain separate artifacts.

sections.heading: Audit findings and the owner response have different authority
sections.text: The June 2025 CPUC audit produced sixteen findings; its letter followed in August. In its response, Gateway claimed fourteen closed and two remaining, with an introductory end-October target. The detailed response instead gives Finding 1 a December 31, 2025 target and Finding 7 an October 24 target. Preserve that discrepancy rather than silently harmonizing the dates. These are operator claims and plans, not independent regulator acceptance or current closure status. The catalog's June 2026 Gateway Generating Station listing concerns a different facility.

sections.heading: The amended contract sets future obligations
sections.text: Resolution E-5428 approved the amended Gateway contract. It sets expected initial delivery for June 1, 2027 and a deadline of August 1, 2027. Neither date is an observed restart or completed delivery. A contract obligation, facility nameplate rating and the capacity actually available during an interval must retain separate meanings; approval of one does not measure the others.

sections.heading: What would resolve the remaining operating question
sections.text: A useful next account needs a final incident disposition, accepted corrective-action and cleanup records, and the exact restored configuration tied to dated service evidence. An operating series should identify its contracted-capacity denominator, reporting intervals, outages and revisions. A missing interval is not a documented zero; partial operation is not full restoration. These are editorial admission requirements, not a claim that agencies or the operator have published nothing further. The earlier saved evidence boundary remains visible below.

retained_open_rail.selected_record: Final investigation and full contracted-capacity restoration
retained_open_rail.statement: The July 25 continuation retained this Open question after earlier partial-return and queue observations. Those saved observations remain evidence with their original dates, not a new queue inspection, a finding of zero operation or a full-restoration decision.

next_artifacts: A final incident disposition and regulator-accepted audit correction record for Gateway Energy Storage, not the similarly named generating station.
A dated cleanup closeout or acceptance artifact, distinct from the order and operator progress claims.
Exact-configuration restoration and recurring service records with contracted capacity, intervals, outages and revisions identified.

records.title: F-35 deliveries and readiness answer different questions
records.answer: F-35 deliveries have grown, but a delivered aircraft, an aircraft accepted with an interim configuration and a mission-ready aircraft are different observations. Current contractor totals and government audits support a detailed account without establishing one monthly factory-productivity measure.
records.scope: One F-35 acquisition and production program. Global program totals, the US operating fleet and Fort Worth line evidence have different populations; aircraft variants, individual jets and supplier parts are not additional projects.
records.stage: Production and delivery documented; capability-state and fleet-readiness measures remain distinct

timeline.event: GAO identifies the program's full-rate production milestone in this month.
The 2025 audit's acceptance and backlog snapshot belongs to this period, not the later publication date.
GAO published its delivery and modernization report.
Lockheed Martin published its calendar-2025 delivery and TR-3 claims.
GAO published the sustainment review covering earlier fiscal-year performance.
The issuer's quarterly and cumulative delivery snapshot ends here; the report was signed later.
GAO published its parts-accountability findings.

sections.heading: Annual deliveries and cumulative inventory are not the same measure
sections.text: Lockheed Martin reports 191 deliveries in calendar 2025. Its later quarterly report records 43 in the quarter ended September 27, 2026 and 1,387 production aircraft delivered since program inception. The quarter is already included in the cumulative total; adding them would double-count aircraft. These are program-wide contractor disclosures, not a Fort Worth-only output series. GAO's March 2024 full-rate production milestone is an acquisition decision, not a measured monthly line rate. None of these quantities measures how often an aircraft can perform its missions.

sections.heading: Lateness depends on what was due and when
sections.text: GAO reports all 110 aircraft delivered in 2024 were late, averaging 238 days. Its May 2025 snapshot records 80 deliveries that year, including 74 due in earlier years. That evidence shows why delivery totals and on-time performance can move differently. It does not identify the backlog-release share of the contractor's eventual full-year total. The recommendation tracker retains July 2026 comments about capacity evaluation and a planned September incentive review; the passage of September is not completion evidence. Read the follow-up page as the same audit's tracker, not another independent finding.

sections.heading: TR-3 claims need an aircraft configuration and date
sections.text: The 2025 audit describes provisional acceptance of non-combat-capable TR-3 aircraft beginning in July 2024 and records 174 such acceptances by May 2025. Lockheed Martin's January 2026 announcement later claims TR-3 completion. Preserve both their sequence and attribution: the later manufacturer statement is not an aircraft-by-aircraft receiving-authority acceptance ledger. It does not independently close every earlier configuration exception or establish completion of the broader Block 4 effort. The useful bridge is the exact configuration accepted, its restrictions and the date those restrictions changed.

sections.heading: Readiness rates describe time and mission scope
sections.text: GAO's June 2026 summary reports mission-capable time declining from 67% in fiscal 2021 to 44% in fiscal 2025, and fully-mission-capable time from 38% to 25%. The first measure concerns at least one tasked mission; the second concerns all missions. These are not the percentages of delivered aircraft that were defective, nor live November readiness readings. The sustainment reset is an improvement strategy with resource and implementation risks, not an observed recovery. A delivery-growth claim and a readiness decline can therefore coexist without referring to the same denominator.

sections.heading: Parts accountability is not a total-loss estimate
sections.text: The November 2026 audit describes roughly 26 million parts valued around $31 billion across more than 700 facilities and identifies incomplete or unreliable accountability records. That inventory value is not a finding that $31 billion of parts is missing. A separate finding concerns unresolved status, as of March 2026, of over $85 million in losses reported earlier. Keep the populations and dates apart. DOD's agreement with the recommendations does not close them; the inspected tracker shows all four Open. Better inventory controls matter, but this audit does not quantify a resulting aircraft availability gain.

sections.heading: A defensible production account needs linked denominators
sections.text: The next useful comparison should connect aircraft due, delivered, formally accepted and held for modification within the same reporting period and production scope. Include configuration, rework and revision treatment before attributing a change to labor or supplier performance. Fleet readiness requires a separate time-based series with its mission definition intact. A missing month is not zero output, and a global total cannot be silently assigned to one line. These are editorial admission criteria; the retained evidence is not erased simply because a complete comparable series remains unresolved.

retained_research.title: Earlier F-35 acceptance and capability evidence
retained_research.text: The July continuation retained the preceding annual delivery and acceptance evidence while leaving the Fort Worth monthly due-versus-accepted series unresolved. Fleet readiness did not substitute for a production-line denominator. This remains an earlier saved decision, not a new July inspection or an admitted monthly series.

retained_research.title: Earlier cross-aircraft comparison decision
retained_research.text: The saved decision rejects a productivity ranking across aircraft programs because delivery, lateness, readiness and governance measures lack a common accepted-output denominator. These new accounts do not reverse that decision.

Comparable fleet-readiness and parts-accountability follow-ups, with mission/time denominators and actual recommendation dispositions preserved.

records.title: KC-46 delivery milestones and the refueling readiness question
records.answer: KC-46 delivery and upgrade milestones are real parts of the program record, but they do not by themselves measure refueling availability. The useful account separates Boeing's period totals, earlier Air Force fleet milestones, test stages and GAO's critique of readiness metrics.

records.scope: The existing, bounded NIST ARIA 0.1 evaluation pilot. The wider ARIA program, future iterations, seven submitted applications and participating organizations are not additional project identities here.
records.stage: Multi-level evaluation pilot; continuous system assurance and operating outcomes remain unadmitted
records.decision_boundary: The established Phase 61 evaluation-before-continuous-assurance stage is retained. The report does not admit a named deployment's authorization, incident response, corrective action or comparable mission outcomes. This review is AI author self-review, not an independent assessment of the evaluated applications.
records.counting_note: This is the same single eligible ARIA 0.1 pilot. Applications, scenarios, organizations and testing sessions are not counted as additional projects.

timeline.event: The pilot report dates the ARIA program launch to May 2024; no exact launch day is supplied in the inspected passage.
The report's publication-history page records NIST Editorial Review Board approval on this day; that is publication review, not system operating authorization.
NIST's publication page dates release of the pilot report to November 13, 2025.

sections.heading: The pilot is the unit of account
sections.text: NIST's publication record identifies five submitting organizations and seven AI applications. It describes three scenarios: TV Spoilers, Meal Planner and Pathfinder. These provide bounded evaluation settings, not a census of operational AI. The portfolio therefore counts the identified pilot once. Neither the number of applications nor the number of scenarios is a measure of deployed systems or public benefit.

sections.heading: Three testing levels answer different questions
sections.text: The program pairs model testing, red teaming and field testing to examine technical and contextual behaviour. Its stated aim is to produce methods and metrics that inform decisions. Our interpretation is that an evaluator should preserve the testing mode with each finding: behaviour under adversarial prompting and behaviour during a user's task are not interchangeable evidence. A program intention is not a completed assurance decision.

sections.heading: Trace the result back to the observation
sections.text: The report connects testing dialogues and questionnaires to assessment and then the Contextual Robustness Index, or CoRIx. The pilot focuses on validity: whether output meets intended-use requirements. Higher reported scores indicate less validity, not a better grade. This makes score direction and the measured construct essential context. We do not turn the instrument into a single general-safety ranking.

sections.heading: Keep coverage limits beside the method
sections.text: The report describes 508 testing sessions and English-language scenarios. Not every application was tested at all three levels; most were submitted for one scenario, and the reported results use a subset. Those limits prevent treating the sessions as a balanced comparison of all applications. Generalising to another language, task or deployment would require evidence beyond this pilot.

sections.heading: A schedule is not a results publication
sections.text: The program homepage still shows a timetable from December 2024 testing through a summer 2025 summary. That schedule is retained as schedule context; the separate publication record dates this report to November 13, 2025. Inspection on November 22, 2026 does not make the report new or verify every scheduled event. Future program plans are not outcomes already achieved.

sections.heading: The missing bridge to operating assurance
sections.text: For a deployed system, our next evidence requirement is an exact application version, use context and owner authorization tied to monitoring, incidents and corrective actions. A meaningful outcome comparison also needs a defined population, baseline and observation period. These are editorial admission criteria, not additional findings from the pilot. The pilot's method can inform that work without substituting for independent review or the owner's operating decision.

next_artifacts: A named system/version evaluation and owner authorization with an explicit use context.
Linked monitoring, incident and corrective-action records rather than a one-off score.
A stable outcome definition, baseline, population and period before comparing mission benefits.

records.title: Moss Landing: battery removal, another fire and separate restart decisions
records.answer: Battery removal at Vistra's Moss Landing site remains distinct from restored storage service. The September 2026 fire involved batteries left in the damaged 300 MW building, not a restarted grid-connected system. Vistra's latest quarterly account keeps the 300 MW and 100 MW facilities in closure and leaves a potential 350 MW restart uncertain.
records.scope: One existing Vistra Moss Landing storage-facility account, distinguishing its 300 MW, 100 MW and 350 MW components. The separate Elkhorn asset, the gas plant and California's wider battery system are outside this project count. Cleanup events do not create new projects.

timeline.event: The fire begins in Vistra's Moss Landing 300 battery building, according to EPA's response record.
EPA's document description dates the agreement under which Vistra performs and pays for battery removal under EPA oversight.

Vistra reports that removal of the final intact batteries has begun; subsequent removal of damaged materials and debris is still described as future work.

sections.heading: A shared site does not have one operating status
sections.text: Vistra's report for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 says the 300 MW and 100 MW batteries will not return to service. It separately describes a potential restart of the 350 MW facility as still under evaluation. These are the operator's component-specific statements, not a declaration that the whole site has restarted. The gas plant and the separate Elkhorn battery cannot supply an operating result for this storage account.

sections.heading: Who is responsible for the cleanup
sections.text: EPA's response page describes Vistra as performing and paying for battery removal under federal oversight. EPA's remit includes removal within the fence and preparation for transport; state and local authorities retain outside-the-fence responsibilities and other on-site matters. The July 17, 2025 agreement therefore establishes a removal obligation and oversight relationship. It is not evidence that all batteries have been removed, that every historical audit item is closed or that the facility is accepted for operation.

sections.heading: The September fire was not a restarted battery service
sections.text: EPA records the September 18 fire in the already damaged Moss Landing 300 building. Its later explanation says the building had no active storage operations and its batteries were not connected to the grid; remaining modules could nevertheless retain charge. EPA describes the exact cause of this September incident as unknown. The incident shows why stopping dispatch and removing a residual fire hazard are different tasks, without establishing a general failure rate for battery storage.

sections.heading: Final phase does not mean finished
sections.text: EPA's September 8 announcement describes demolition and treatment of previously inaccessible material and projects removal and demolition completion in mid-2027. That is a forecast. Vistra's November 12 update says removal of the final intact batteries has begun, with damaged material and debris to follow. These statements concern different work packages and dates. Neither should be compressed into a completed-cleanup claim or used to award an operating-recovery stage.

sections.heading: Monitoring and laboratory samples need separate interpretation
sections.text: EPA's September-fire FAQ reports perimeter monitoring for particular pollutants and describes additional sampling. Vistra's September 29 update reports nickel slightly above the applicable screening level at one southwest location during the shelter-in-place period, followed by samples without exceedances after the order ended. These are different measures and time windows. The operator's account is attributed, not independently confirmed here: the county page returned HTTP 403. Neither account establishes a site-wide health outcome or an absence of all exposure.

sections.heading: An investigation update is not regulatory acceptance
sections.text: EPA's historical timeline retains a January-entry statement that the cause was being investigated. Vistra's later quarterly filing says its own fire investigation was completed during the third quarter, while still leaving the 350 MW restart uncertain. This does not provide a regulator's causal finding, close the distinct September incident or authorize operation. The next useful records are authority-reviewed findings, documented removal/disposal completion and any component-specific restart acceptance, followed by comparable operating observations.

records.title: Manatee storage: capacity, monthly operation and a changing battery fleet
records.answer: Manatee is an existing, owner-reported in-service battery, not just an announced capacity project. Its 409 MW power rating and 900 MWh energy rating describe different capabilities. The retained monthly record provides operating evidence, while interval availability, measured customer savings and the original retirement proposal remain separate questions.
records.scope: One Florida Power & Light battery facility at Parrish, Manatee County, Florida. The adjacent solar facility, older thermal units, other FPL batteries and the Florida utility-storage system are related but distinct objects. The EIA plant label used in the earlier monthly acquisition does not turn every resource at the site into this battery.
records.stage: Owner-reported in service; retained monthly evidence; interval availability remains unresolved

timeline.event: FPL announced that construction had begun and described anticipated storage, savings and retirement benefits. These were prospective claims at that date.
FPL announced commissioning and described the battery as newly operational, with 409 MW of power and 900 MWh of stored energy.
The 2026–2035 site plan was submitted to the Florida Public Service Commission. Its battery-storage narrative retains Manatee's end-2021 in-service history; the plan is not a new commissioning event.
The inspected EIA release index dates publication of August 2026 monthly data here. This is a dataset-release date, not an additional Manatee operating observation in this account.
FPL announced commissioning of the separate Lansing Smith battery and called it the company's largest by energy capacity. The announcement changes fleet context, not Manatee's identity or rating.

sections.heading: Power and stored energy answer different questions
sections.text: FPL describes Manatee as a 409 MW / 900 MWh battery at Parrish, charged from the nearby Manatee Solar Energy Center. MW measures rated power; MWh measures stored energy. Dividing the two published ratings gives about 2.20 hours at rated power as nameplate arithmetic, not a measured discharge test or an availability guarantee. The owner's household-equivalent illustration depends on assumed household demand and should not be treated as the number of customers continuously served. The solar plant and battery have different functions even when their location and charging relationship are shared.

sections.heading: Commissioning does not settle the retirement account
sections.text: The January 2021 construction announcement linked the battery and other modernization work to anticipated retirement of older gas units, fuel savings and emissions reductions. FPL's December announcement then established an owner-reported commissioning milestone. It did not establish all the forecast benefits. The April 2026 plan's note on Manatee Units 1 and 2 describes them as winter-peaking units staffed and operated for extreme winter demand. That later qualification matters: the earlier retirement proposal is not proof that both units were permanently retired. No measured avoided-emissions or customer-savings total is derived here.

sections.heading: Read fleet plans with their reporting dates
sections.text: The April 2026 plan describes 991 MW of large-scale installed battery storage across FPL's system, including Manatee and other facilities. That is a fleet snapshot in a planning document, not Manatee's available power or a statewide outcome. Later installations can change the fleet total without changing this facility's identity. The plan's future additions are forecasts; they must not be counted as already operating assets or used as a denominator for Manatee's performance.

sections.heading: Monthly data are evidence, but not an availability series
sections.text: The earlier monthly acquisition is retained below with its actual July review date. It should not be erased by describing all operating evidence as missing. EIA's current release index covers monthly and annual plant-level statistics and, on this inspection, lists August 2026 data released on October 23. The ZIP workbook was not newly extracted in this review, so this account does not add June–August observations or certify revisions to the earlier months. Charging energy, gross output and reported net generation are different fields; their names and reporting periods must be preserved before comparing values.

sections.heading: A larger energy store is not a larger power rating
sections.text: On November 9, 2026, FPL described the separate Lansing Smith facility as 400 MW and 1,600 MWh, with up to four hours of supply. Its claim to be FPL's largest battery by stored-energy capacity is compatible with Manatee's higher 409 MW power rating and lower 900 MWh energy rating. Comparing MWh with MW would produce a false ranking. The new announcement neither expands Manatee nor establishes a global league table. Historical superlatives remain attached to their date and metric, and Lansing Smith is context only in this account.

sections.heading: The next evidence must measure the service being claimed
sections.text: A current rating and monthly totals do not answer whether the battery was available during particular peak intervals, how often it was constrained, or how benefits were allocated to customers. The next useful review should join the exact battery identity to dated interval dispatch and outage or availability records, with a declared denominator and revision policy. It should keep a missing interval separate from a documented zero. Any savings or emissions claim needs a stated comparison case rather than conversion of a construction forecast into a measured result. These are editorial evidence requirements, not a finding that those records do not exist.

retained_evidence.statement: The retained July 25 acquisition identified the energy-storage worksheet's Manatee Solar Energy Center row, plant 60014, and recorded monthly charging energy, gross generation and reported net generation for January–May 2026. It moved that evidence gap to Partially Closed, while interval dispatch and availability remained unresolved. Those are earlier saved findings, not a new workbook inspection or a new governed operating-series admission.

next_artifacts: The current EIA energy-storage worksheet for the exact plant/battery identity, with a preserved release vintage and an explicit comparison against the retained January–May record.
Named-battery interval dispatch, outage and availability evidence with stable reporting periods, denominators and revision treatment.
Dated unit-disposition and measured cost or emissions evidence before replacing the earlier modernization forecasts with outcome claims.

The existing July 25 monthly acquisition remains Partially Closed; this account neither downgrades it to no evidence nor upgrades it to interval availability. records.answer: Gateway's record includes commissioning, a serious fire, cleanup requirements and a documented partial return to service. Those milestones answer different questions. The unresolved question is full contracted-capacity restoration and its supporting operating record, not whether any operation ever resumed.
